The Hedging Policy must clearly define the decision-making process, which is generally based on two key bodies, pillars of the risk governance structure, namely the Board of Directors or its equivalent management body, and the Steering Committee.

**a. The Board of Directors or Equivalent Management Body**
The "Hedging Policy" document must be approved by the Board of Directors or its equivalent management body.

**b. The Steering Committee**
The Steering Committee is responsible for the implementation of the Hedging Policy, the validation, and the supervision of the risk management strategy. It is necessary to establish a clear delegation of responsibilities from the Steering Committee within a framework document that also sets out the composition of the Committee.
The Committee must include departments whose involvement allows for a good assessment of the level of risk exposure, preferably the Finance and Treasury Department, the Procurement Department, the Commercial Department, and the Department responsible for Risk Management.
The Committee reports to the Board of Directors or the equivalent management body on a periodic basis.
The Steering Committee must ensure that market risk analysis and management activities are carried out by personnel possessing the required technical knowledge and experience in the field of financial risks and hedging instruments.
A continuous and targeted training policy for human resources involved in risk management is essential to ensure good know-how and to keep pace with rapid market developments. It is also important to equip the structures involved in risk management with appropriate technical means for monitoring markets and evaluating hedging instruments. **N°94 -13 OF SEPTEMBER 7, 1994**

**SUBJECT: Importation, sale, reconversion, and re-exportation of foreign currency by travelers.**

The purpose of this circular is to recall the conditions for the importation, deposit, and sale of foreign currency by travelers and to establish the procedures for the sale, reconversion, and re-exportation of said foreign currency by non-resident travelers.

**Article 1:** Travelers may freely import instruments or means of payment denominated in foreign currency without any amount limitations.

**Article 2:** Travelers are required to deposit the foreign currency in their possession with Authorized Intermediaries.
However, non-resident travelers are authorized to keep the imported foreign currency themselves to cover their expenses in Tunisia.

**Article 3:** Travelers are required to sell the foreign currency in their possession to Authorized Intermediaries or to exchange sub-delegates, in all cases where this sale is prescribed.

**Article 4:** Authorized Intermediaries and exchange sub-delegates are authorized to purchase foreign currency without requiring justification of the origin or identity of the seller. However, they are required in all cases to provide the seller with a numbered receipt indicating, in particular, the name of the Authorized Intermediary, the type of currency, the exchange rate applied, the counter-value in dinars, and the date of the sale.
At the request of the seller, this receipt must be replaced by an exchange slip which must mention, in particular, their identity and passport number; the type of currency sold, its amount (in letters and figures) and its counter-value in dinars; the date of sale, the origin of the foreign currency (debit from a foreign account, transfer, check, money order, physical import, etc.) and the last b) - upon presentation of a slip constituting an authorization for the export of foreign currency, if this currency was received from abroad by cheque, transfer, or money order or any other instrument of debt, or if it originates from the debit of a foreign account in foreign currency;

c) - upon presentation of the customs-endorsed import declaration for foreign currency, if the amount to be re-exported was physically imported from abroad and is equal to or greater than the equivalent of 5,000 D.T.

Article 10: Non-resident travelers may also re-export foreign currency resulting from the reconversion of dinars obtained by the exchange of foreign currency, upon presentation of:

a) - the exchange slip and the exchange receipt referred to in Articles 4 and 8 above, if the amount to be re-exported is less than the equivalent of 5,000 D.T., or if the foreign currency used to acquire the dinars was received from abroad by cheque, transfer, or money order or any other instrument of debt, or originates from the debit of a foreign account in convertible foreign currency or dinars.

b) - the aforementioned exchange slip and exchange receipt, as well as the customs-endorsed import declaration for foreign currency, if the amount to be re-exported is equal to or greater than the equivalent of 5,000 D.T. and originates from the exchange of foreign currency physically imported by the non-resident traveler.

Article 10 bis2: In all cases provided for by this circular, the amount of foreign currency to be physically exported cannot exceed the equivalent of thirty thousand dinars (30,000 D) per trip. **No. 87-25 OF JULY 17, 1987**

**SUBJECT: Granting of Sub-Delegate Status for Currency Exchange and Conditions for Exercising Sub-Delegation.**

The purpose of this circular is, on the one hand, to authorize sub-delegates to carry out manual currency exchange by purchasing foreign currency against dinars, and on the other hand, to introduce relaxations regarding the conditions for granting and exercising sub-delegation, particularly by eliminating the prior authorization of the Central Bank of Tunisia for the granting of sub-delegate status.

It repeals and replaces Circular No. 85-31 and Note No. 85-66 of September 4, 1985.

**I - GENERAL PROVISIONS**

**Article 1:** Apart from Approved Intermediaries and customs offices authorized for this purpose, only persons who have previously obtained a sub-delegation from an Approved Intermediary may accept foreign banknotes and traveler's checks carried by non-resident Tunisian or foreign travelers.

**Article 2:** Individuals or legal entities, including hotels, travel agencies, and craft product sales shops, who, due to the nature of their activity, are likely to receive means of payment expressed in foreign currency from non-resident travelers, are authorized to receive sub-delegations.

**Article 3:** Sub-delegation authorizes its holder to:

1°) Accept the settlement of purchases or services by non-residents through the transfer of foreign currency.

2°) Carry out manual currency exchange by purchasing foreign currency against the delivery of dinars.

Sub-delegates are in no case authorized to issue foreign currency.

[Footnote: 1 See BCT circular to I.A. No. 97-07 of May 9, 1997]

**II - GRANTING OF SUB-DELEGATIONS**

**Artic** **Article 12:** The proceeds from foreign currency sales carried out by the sub-delegate shall be credited to its account opened with the authorized delegate intermediary.

The notebooks used for carrying out such operations must be kept by the sub-delegate for a period of 10 years.

**IV - RELATIONS BETWEEN SUB-DELEGATED ESTABLISHMENTS AND THEIR CLIENTELE**

**Article 13:** For each exchange transaction, the sub-delegate shall complete a dual-copy slip from the stub notebook. Each transaction must be recorded by duplication or carbon copy on both the original, which will be given to the seller, and the copy.

For any canceled transaction, the original must be attached to the stub.

**Article 14:** Sub-delegated establishments must identify themselves by posting a sign at the counter stating: "Establishment authorized to receive foreign currency under sub-delegation from the Authorized Intermediary (name of I.A.T.)".

Similarly, the following must be made known to the clientele by posting:

1°) The exchange rates at which the counter-value in Dinars of the means of payment susceptible to being negotiated in accordance with the instructions of the Authorized Delegate Intermediary will be discounted.

In this regard, it should be recalled that, in accordance with the current foreign exchange regulations, sub-delegates may only apply to the clientele for the purchase of foreign banknotes and traveler's checks the buying rate in effect on the day the transaction is carried out, as published by the Central Bank of Tunisia.

2°) The obligation to hand over the original of the slip extracted from the stub notebook to the presenter.

3°) The prohibition for any employee other than the head of exchange to cash or exchange foreign banknotes and traveler's checks. **APPENDIX I TO CIRCULAR TO AUTHORIZED INTERMEDIARIES N°87-25 OF JULY 17, 1987**

**Subject:** Granting of Sub-Delegate Status for Foreign Exchange and Conditions for Exercising Sub-Delegation.

**Reference:** Circular to Authorized Intermediaries no. 87-25 of July 17, 1987.

Article 2 of the aforementioned circular lists the individuals who can benefit from the status of sub-delegate for foreign exchange, stating that "natural persons or legal entities, particularly hoteliers, travel agencies, and handicraft product shops, who, due to the nature of their activity, are called upon to receive payment methods expressed in foreign currency from non-resident travelers, are authorized to receive sub-delegations."

CIRCULAR TO LICENSED INTERMEDIARY BANKS N°2008-04 OF MARCH 03, 2008

Subject: Carrying out manual foreign exchange activity

Article 1: Licensed intermediary banks may, in accordance with current legislation, carry out manual foreign exchange activity within specialized agencies called "bureaux de change" (exchange offices).

Article 2: The opening of exchange offices is subject to the conditions set out in Annex n°1 of this circular. These conditions constitute minimum requirements.

Article 3: Licensed intermediary banks must declare to the Central Bank of Tunisia, according to the models provided in Annexes n°2 and n°3 of this circular, any operation of opening or closing an exchange office at least fifteen (15) working days in advance of the date of opening or closing.

It is prohibited to use the premises, subject to closure, for carrying out any operation with customers.

Article 4: The provisions of the preceding article apply to any operation of temporary or definitive transfer of an exchange office.

Article 5: Bank branches and exchange offices, established in the zones determined in Annex n°4 of this circular, must provide foreign exchange services outside ordinary working hours, including during public holidays, in accordance with on-call schedules among them which determine, in particular, the hours during which these services must be provided.
The Central Bank of Tunisia shall set the said schedule and inform bank branches and exchange offices of it.

Article 6: Exchange offices must display to the public, using visible electronic displays, the exchange rates in dinars applied to the sale and purchase operations with customers of foreign banknotes and traveler's checks. **APPENDIX N°1 TO CIRCULAR TO APPROVED INTERMEDIARY BANKS N°2008-04**

**CONDITIONS FOR OPENING FOREIGN EXCHANGE OFFICES**

Approved intermediary banks must comply with the following conditions when opening a foreign exchange office:

**Article 1:** The foreign exchange office premises must be visible and identifiable to the public.

To this end, the term "foreign exchange office" must be displayed on the facade of the foreign exchange office.

**Article 2:** Approved intermediary banks must take all security measures relating to the protection of persons and the premises of the foreign exchange office.

They must ensure that the premises are permanently connected to the police station by means of a special telephone line.

**Article 3:** Approved intermediary banks must have a procedures manual relating to the security of foreign exchange office premises, specifically describing police alert procedures in case of justified concerns or aggression. The procedures manual must be made available to the agents of the foreign exchange office.

Approved intermediary banks must also implement training programs for these agents.

**Article 4:** The foreign exchange office must be permanently connected to the bank's headquarters by all means of communication and data exchange. ANNEX 2 TO CIRCULAR 2008-04 TO APPROVED INTERMEDIARY BANKS

**No. 2002-17 of August 5, 2002**

**SUBJECT: Verification of the identity of travel check holders.**

It has been brought to my attention that certain authorized intermediaries and sub-delegates of exchange have cashed travel checks for foreign tourists by referring, for the verification of these tourists' identity, to passports other than those used for entry into Tunisia.

Consequently, and to avoid the risks of fraud that could be committed by travelers holding travel checks, such as the presentation of forged travel checks for payment, authorized intermediaries are required to refer, for the purpose of verifying the identity of these persons, to passports bearing the entry stamp into Tunisia and to inform the sub-delegates of exchange carrying out exchange operations on their behalf of these provisions. **Article 1:** Any Tunisian national who is a natural person residing in Tunisia and intends to engage in manual currency exchange activities by opening a currency exchange office must first obtain authorization from the Central Bank of Tunisia. This requires submitting a written application, in accordance with the model in Annex No. 1 of this circular, to the head office of the Bank, against a receipt. The application must be accompanied by the following documents:

*   A copy of the national identity card;
*   A certified true copy of a certificate of training in manual currency exchange issued to the applicant by the Academy of Banks and Finance, under the Tunisian Professional Association of Banks and Financial Institutions;
*   The original of a first-demand bank guarantee issued according to the model in Annex No. 2 of this circular, in favor of the Central Bank of Tunisia, for an amount of fifty thousand dinars (50,000 D);
*   A criminal record certificate (bulletin n°3) dated less than three months from the date of the authorization application submission;
*   A certificate of non-bankruptcy dated less than three months from the date of the authorization application submission;
*   Sixth item (amended by Circular No. 2019-07 of October 14, 2019): a lease agreement or proof of ownership of the premises, a business lease management contract, or a temporary occupation contract for premises under the public domain regime, intended for carrying out manual currency exchange activities. The premises reserved for the currency exchange office must be visible, identifiable by the public, and located in an easily accessible site, far from constructions and equipment that could present a risk.

**Second New Paragraph** (amended by Circular No. 2019‑07 of 14 October 2019):  
A natural person authorized to carry out manual currency‑exchange activities through one or more exchange bureaus may open only one “exchange‑bureau account” per currency, and may open “exchange‑bureau accounts” only with a single approved intermediary.

For the opening of an “exchange‑bureau account,” the approved intermediary must require a sworn declaration in which the natural person concerned states that he/she does not have any “exchange‑bureau account” opened with another approved intermediary.

---

**Article 10 – First New Paragraph** (amended by Circular No. 2019‑07 of 14 October 2019):  

The “exchange‑bureau account” is freely credited by the deposit of foreign banknotes purchased by the exchange bureau (or bureaus) belonging to the same natural‑person account holder, as well as by the interest earned on the amounts placed in these accounts, calculated in accordance with the conditions set out by the applicable regulations.

The account is freely debited by the withdrawal of foreign banknotes for the exclusive needs of the exchange‑bureau activity, by the sale of foreign currency to an approved intermediary, and by investment operations carried out in conformity with the applicable regulations.

When an “exchange‑bureau account” shows a credit balance exceeding the equivalent of five hundred thousand dinars (500,000 dinars), taking into account the amount currently placed, the account holder must, no later than two working days after the occurrence, arrange – through the banks – the sale of the amount exceeding this ceiling in exchange for dinars.

Any other credit or debit operation on the “exchange‑bureau account” is subject to authorization by the Central Bank of Tunisia, and the account may under no circumstances be allowed to become overdrawn.

---

**Article 11 – New** (text continues…) **Article 12:** A natural person authorized to carry out manual foreign exchange activities through a currency exchange office who intends to cease their activity must inform the Central Bank of Tunisia in advance, using the model in Annex No. 5, by any means leaving a written record.

The cessation of activity must immediately result in the closure of the "currency exchange office accounts" in foreign currency by the authorization holder, and the sale of their credit balances in exchange for the dinar.

**Article 13:** The authorization to carry out manual foreign exchange activities through a currency exchange office shall be withdrawn by the Central Bank of Tunisia in the following cases:

1.  Non-compliance with the conditions for conducting manual foreign exchange operations as set forth in the present circular and in the current foreign exchange regulations.
2.  Failure to meet any of the conditions for carrying out the activity under which the authorization was granted.
3.  The natural person authorized to carry out manual foreign exchange activities through a currency exchange office does not effectively engage in their activity within the period specified in Article 2 of the present circular. **ANNEX N°1**

**OBJECT: Manual exchange.**

Law No. 85‑108 of 6 December 1985, which encourages financial and banking institutions that work essentially with non‑residents, has broadened the scope of activity of these institutions by authorising them, in particular, to carry out manual foreign‑exchange transactions for their non‑resident clientele under the conditions set by the Central Bank of Tunisia. ### 1) Manual exchange

Pursuant to Article 6 of Law No. 85‑108, non‑resident banks are authorised to perform manual foreign‑exchange operations on behalf of their non‑resident clients who hold foreign‑currency accounts opened on their books.

For this purpose, they are permitted to hold cash in dinars and in foreign currency. This cash is replenished in dinars by:

* sales of foreign currency to the Central Bank of Tunisia,

It is replenished in foreign currency by their purchases of foreign banknotes from the Central Bank of Tunisia or from the bank’s non‑resident clientele.

The Authorized Intermediary shall not sell currencies to the client at the spot market or within the framework of a hedging operation on behalf of an operator holding funds in his professional currency accounts or open positions on the books of other Authorized Intermediaries, except up to the amount required for uncovered settlement.

Subject: Opening accounts abroad

Article 1: Resident enterprises holding foreign markets with the objective of providing services or carrying out works for non-residents are authorized to open freely accounts with banks in the countries where the markets are realized, in the national currency of that country, which shall be used for housing the portion of the price of these markets intended for local expenses.

This measure applies exclusively to markets realized in foreign countries whose legislation and regulation provide for the obligation to settle the portion of the price intended for local expenses in the national currency of these countries and the other part in convertible currencies.

Article 2: Any enterprise having carried out the opening of such a type of account shall inform the Bank of Tunisia (Direction of Analysis and Follow-up of Transfer and External Commerce Operations) of this operation and submit a copy of the related contract within a ten-day working period following the opening date of the account.

Article 3: At the end of the execution of the contract, the resident enterprise is obliged to close any account opened abroad in local currency in relation to this market and repatriate the credit balance of this account. OBJECT: Financial regulation for imports and exports of merchandise.

The present circular aims to set the conditions and modalities for the financial regulation of imports and exports of merchandise.

CHAPTER ONE
GENERAL PROVISIONS

It is carried out in conformity with the stipulations of the commercial contract and according to the conditions defined by the present circular.

Article 2, first paragraph (new): The domiciliation of titles of foreign trade, invoices for export, commercial invoices, and, for imports subject to Article Article 6 (new) 3: Subject to the provisions of articles 7 and 8 bis, customs regulations shall be carried out after the effective entry of merchandises into Tunisia, proven by the customs declaration submitted to the approved intermediary.

The approved intermediary carries out transfers within the limits of customs declarations and final invoices required by customs.

Article 7 (new) 3: The approved intermediary is authorized to carry out advance payments or settlements, required by the supplier under the commercial contract, on behalf of the resident importer, upon the supplier's bank's request for a guarantee of the refund of the payment amount.

Article 9: The financial settlement for imported packaging to be filled and reexported, and for merchandise imported into Tunisia for reexport after active processing, may be made under the commercial contract subject to the following conditions:

SUBJECT: Transfers related to current operations concerning international transport.

GENERAL PROVISIONS

In accordance with the first article of the Code des Changes as amended by Law No. 93-48 of May 1993, commitments in matters of current operations and the resulting transfers are free. The present circular aims to establish the conditions and modalities for Intermediaries Agreed to carry out transfers related to current operations concerning international transport and to define the applicable rules regarding transport operators' revenues and expenses.

FIRST TITLE
MARITIME TRANSPORT
FIRST CHAPTER
REGULATIONS ON CHARTERING OF NON-RESIDENT SHIPS

The rules resulting from chartering contracts of non-resident ships, including, if applicable, advances and commissions in favor of non-resident brokers, are carried out by Intermediaries Agreed in accordance with the indications of the Ministry in charge of Merchant Navy, as stated in the reserved form*.

FIRST CHAPTER 2
REVENUES OF NON-RESIDENT MARITIME COMPANIES ON PASSENGER, BAGGAGE, AND V 3) Consignators shall open on their account books, in the name of each non-resident shipowner, a Non-resident Shipowner Account intended to record the receipts and expenses effectively received or incurred during Tunisian port calls of vessels whose consignment they have been entrusted with.

The Non-resident Shipowner Account shall be kept in such a way that all receipts and expenses related to a single port call can be traced at any moment.

PARAGRAPH 1ST
RULES OF OPERATION FOR THE NON-RESIDENT SHIPOWNER ACCOUNT
A) Credit Operations
The following are debited to the account:
- freight payments for cargo on behalf of importers or exporters (FOB import, CF export, etc.);
- advances made on behalf of non-residents by:
  * exporters or transitors, in accordance with the freight of exported goods;
  * transitors, in accordance with the freight of transiting international goods;

Exporters and transitors must repay the amount of these advances within a maximum period of 3 months from the date they were made to the consignator of the ships.

- advances for port charges of the non-resident shipowner's vessels;
These advances are settled to the consignators either A) Repayment of the debtor's balance
When the cleared balance on the account at the date of the arrest is a debt for the ship's owner, the amount of this debt must be repaid no later than one month after the date of the arrest of the account, unless it is covered, before the expiration of this period, by the registration of other receipts to the credit of the account.

B) Settlements among ship owners' agents representing the same non-resident shipowner

Without prejudice to the preceding provisions, ship owners' agents representing the same non-resident shipowner may, upon instructions from the latter, proceed with compensation between the debtor balances and the creditor balances of the said shipowner.

SECTION 2
REVENUES AND EXPENSES OF RESIDENT SHIPOWNERS

1°) Resident shipowners must be represented in every country of destination of their ships, except where they have their own offices of representation, by one or more agents (ship owners' agents or any other agent to whom the ship consignment may be entrusted) charged with collecting receipts and engaging expenses of call for the said ships in one of the ports of that country.

2°) The expenses of any call of ships of a resident shipowner can be settled through receipts collected by the same representative for that call or 2) Repatriation of the creditor's balance

When the cleared balance is in favor of the resident shipowner, the amount of this balance should be repatriated no later than one month after the date of the position's arrest, unless it is used before the expiration of this delay to cover other port expenses.

3) Settlements between the foreign representatives of a resident shipowner

Without prejudice to the preceding provisions, the representatives of a resident shipowner in the same foreign country may, upon instructions from the latter, proceed with compensation between the debtor balances and the creditor balances of their respective positions regarding said shipowner.

CHAPTER 4
COMMON EXPLOITATION OF SHIPS BY RESIDENT AND NON-RESIDENT SHIPOWNERS

1) In the context of the common exploitation of ships with non-resident shipowners, resident shipowners may make settlements in favor of these last ones, either in the form of profit distribution or of their contribution to the exploitation charges. The result of the exploitation must be settled at least once a year.

Transfers related to these settlements are made by the Designated Intermediaries, upon presentation:
- of the association contract subject to approval by the Ministry in charge of Merchant Marine,
- and of a signed and certified statement conforming to the accounting records by the resident A) Credit Operations

These advances to the credit account are recorded upon presentation of all relevant documents justifying the importation of currencies (credit memos, banking statements, etc.).

B) Debit Operations

Expenses incurred by non-resident road transport operators in Tunisia are recorded as debits on the account, including but not limited to:
- port fees (mooring, transit, container stationing fees, etc.) ;
- cargo handling fees (loading and unloading of trucks, semi-trailers, or containers, grouping, de-grouping, warehousing, etc.) ;
- vehicle expenses (circulation taxes, towing fees, repair costs, and vehicle part purchases, etc.) ;
- services rendered to drivers (medical expenses, hospitalization, and repatriation, etc.) ;
- agency fees (representative commissions, etc.) ;
- any other expense related to the non-resident road transport operator's ongoing operations in Tunisia.

PARAGRAPH 2
SETTLEMENT OF NON-RESIDENT TIR ACCOUNT

Representatives in Tunisia of non-resident road transport operators must settle the balance of any open TIR Non-resident account on their books no later than three months following its opening or the last date it was settled. They may transfer the credit balance 3) Resident road transporters must keep a record of all receipts collected and expenses incurred by their representatives abroad. This record shall be kept in such a way that all receipts and expenses related to a single journey can be traced at any moment.

PARAGRAPH 1
JOURNEY RECEIPTS AND EXPENSES

A) Journey receipts

The journey receipts of resident road transporters' vehicles abroad are composed of:
- transport charges and accessory receipts;
- advances made by resident road transporters to their representatives abroad for travel expenses.

B) Travel expenses

The following are considered travel expenses abroad for resident road transporters' vehicles:
- port charges (mooring, transit, stationing fees for trucks, semi-trailers or containers, etc.);
- cargo charges (loading and unloading of trucks, semi-trailers or containers, grouping or de-grouping, etc.);
- vehicle expenses (circulation taxes, traction fees, repair costs and prices of spare parts for vehicles, fuels and lubricants, etc.);
- services rendered to drivers (medical expenses, hospitalization, repatriation, etc.);
- agency fees (representative commissions, etc.). The transfers under these regulations are carried out by Authorized Intermediaries, upon presentation of:
- of the common exploitation agreement, as prescribed by the transport terrestrial ministry,
- and of a signed and certified statement by the railway transport company resident, indicating the collected receipts and incurred expenses by each transport company, the operating result and its distribution.

2°) The amounts due to railway transport companies residents by non-resident railway transport companies, in regard to the distribution of the net operating result, must be repatriated no later than one month following their due date.

CHAPTER 3
INTERNATIONAL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAIL

REGULATIONS BETWEEN MAGHREB RAILWAY TRANSPORT COMPANIES

The transfers under these regulations, in favor of one of the Maghreb railway transport companies, by the Tunisian National Railways, are carried out by Authorized Intermediaries, upon presentation of an extract duly certified by this last one from the companies' accounts established by the Maghreb Central Compensation Bureau, indicating the compensated amounts, the resulting balances, and the payable amount.

Article 1: The present circular sets out the conditions and modalities for the realization by Intermediaries Agreed for transfers under the title of fees related to professional training abroad, namely the registration and training fees, installation fees, and living expenses.

Article 2 (repealed and replaced by Article 1 of the circular to I.A. No. 2023-03 of June 30, 2023): Any person residing in France desiring to pursue training abroad may benefit from transfers under the title of professional training fees abroad.

OBJECT: Tourist Allocation

Article 1: The following circulatory sets out the conditions and modalities for implementation by Intermediaries Approved for transfers regarding the tourist allocation.

SECTION 1
BENEFICIARIES OF THE ALLOCATION

Article 2: Eligible for the delivery of the tourist allocation are:

1) Travelers holding the status of residents according to the regulations on changes, in possession of a valid ordinary passport.
2) Tunisian students or trainees pursuing their studies abroad, holding a valid ordinary passport, and whose parents have the status of residents in Tunisia.
3) Tunisians who were non-residents according to the regulations on changes and have returned definitively to Tunisia, regardless of the duration of their stay in Tunisia after said return.

The definitive return can be proven by any official document (consular attestation, document attesting the benefit of a customs duty exemption for household goods or vehicles…).

SECTION II
AMOUNT OF THE ALLOCATION
Article 3: The amount of the tourist allocation is set at the sum of six thousand dinars Article 11: The traveler must keep the formule "A" for proof of the origin of the currency or checks they possess before leaving Tunisia, presented to customs. Formule "B" is to be kept by the Accredited Intermediary. Formule "C" is an authorization to export the means of payment (species or checks) provided by the Accredited Intermediary; it is to be handed to customs upon exit from Tunisian territory.

Article 12: Accredited Intermediaries must:

a) assign a numbered order to the three formulas and write this number on each of them in the designated space. The formule "A" (the copy to be kept by the traveler) must be in original and completely legible.

b) fill in the relevant sections of these formulas, including those concerning the traveler's identity, their national identity card or residence permit number, the method of allocation of the tourist allowance, the number and denomination of the coupons issued, and, if applicable, the reference section for the specific authorization issued by the Central Bank of Tunisia.

c) remove formule "B" and keep it available for the Central Bank of Tunisia for control purposes.

Article 13: Any beneficiary of a tourist allowance granted in cash and following a genuine journey abroad Article 19: In case of return of an international payment card, the Approved Intermediary is obliged to indicate on the passport the rights still inscribed on the card.

SECTION IV
MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS

Article 20: Approved Intermediaries must ensure that the conditions for issuing the allocation are met by each person requesting it. For this purpose, in addition to the passport, they must request the national identity card from Tunisian nationals and the residence permit from foreign nationals.

Article 21: No allocation can be given to a traveler carrying an expired passport, even if, in accordance with police regulations, crossing the border of the destination country is not subject to the presentation of a valid passport.

Article 22: For a tourist allocation of six thousand dinars (6,000 D), foreign nationals must sign a declaration on honor according to the model in Annex 1 of this circular bearing the signature and stamp of the Approved Intermediary, as well as the same indications as those on the concerned passport regarding the tourist allocation (amount, country of destination, civil year...). It should be addressed to the Central Bank of Tunisia at the same time as the monthly statements of tourist allocations, as provided for in Article 27 of this circular. Subject: Procedures for the delivery of tourist allocations by Approved Intermediaries.

It has come to my attention that certain Approved Intermediaries do not take the necessary precautions when granting tourist allocations by delivering currencies to persons other than the passport holders.

Therefore, the attention of Approved Intermediaries is drawn to the fact that any applicant for a tourist allocation must present himself in person at the bank counter with his passport and sign the forms A, B and C referred to in the annexes 1, 2, 3 and 4 of Circular No. 2007-04 of February 9, 2007 on the tourist allocation, in the presence of the counter clerk.

The Approved Intermediary must also keep in accessible files, in addition to form B intended for him, copies of the two pages of the passport bearing the traveler's identity and the object of the tourist allocation granted.

SUBJECT: Transfers for Medical Treatment and Related Accommodation Fees Abroad

The present circular aims to set out the modalities for the Intermediaries Agreed for transfers of medical treatment and accommodation fees abroad for patients and their potential companions, regardless of their nature.

SECTION 1
TRANSFER OF HEALTH CARE COSTS
1°) For patients not covered by an insurance or social security institution:

Transfers for health care costs are made upon presentation of invoices or definitive bills from the non-resident service provider (doctor, medical establishment, laboratory, etc.) and the original medical certificate, issued by a specialist doctor established in Tunisia, indicating the nature of the treatments (consultation, hospitalization, surgeries, specialized analyses, etc.), the name of the foreign service provider, the identity of the patient's companion (if applicable), and, if necessary, the need for the patient's evacuation by a medical transport means.

However, if payments are made before the start of the treatments, the patient may transfer:
- the amount indicated by the foreign service provider. 2) For the benefit of companions:
"The patient going abroad for medical treatments other than a cure, can be accompanied by one person who can transfer up to One Thousand Dinars (1,000D) per journey."1.

The delivery of currencies is made by the Approved Intermediary with whom the file for transfer of healthcare and related costs is constituted, based on:
- when the patient is not taken charge, of the original of the medical certificate mentioned in Section I, 1° above, indicating the companion's identity;
- when the patient is taken charge, of the decision to take charge of the patient intended for the Approved Intermediary. If the companion's identity, other than those mentioned in Section I, 2° above, is not indicated in the decision to take charge, the transfer can be made upon presentation, in addition to the said decision, of an attestation indicating the companion's identity established either by the insurer or social security institution or by the patient's treating doctor.

The Approved Intermediary will note accordingly the companion's passport by affixing a stamp that shows the amount, nature, and date of the service provided.

In accordance with Decree No. 2000-133 of January 18, 2000, regarding the establishment of a sales regime to non-residents with VAT restitution, non-resident foreign nationals are granted the possibility of being refunded the VAT on their local or imported purchases that accompany their departure from Tunisian territory by air or sea, provided that these purchases are made by credit card.

In accordance with this decree, a non-resident is considered to be any person of foreign nationality residing abroad whose stay in Tunisia does not exceed three months at the time of departure.

- merchants who can operate under this regime are obliged, upon realization of each VAT-taxable sales operation, to collect the VAT amount and issue a sales invoice in duplicate,

In light of Circular No. 2013-15 of November 7, 2013 implementing internal control rules for managing the risk of money laundering and terrorist financing;
In light of Decision No. 2017-01 of the Tunisian Financial Analysis Commission of March 2, 2017 on the principles related to the declaration of suspicious operations and transactions;
In light of Decision No. 2017-02 of the Tunisian Financial Analysis Commission of March 2, 2017 on the principles for financial professions regarding the detection and declaration of suspicious operations and transactions;
In light of Decision No. 2017-03 of the Tunisian Financial Analysis Commission of March 2, 2017 on effective beneficiaries;
In light of 1. "significant shareholder or associate": an shareholder or associate holding 10% or more of the capital of the corporate client.
2. "effective beneficiary": any natural person who ultimately owns or controls the corporate client or for whose account the transaction is carried out without the need for a written power of attorney between the client and the effective beneficiary.
3. "Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs)": natural persons who have held or have been holding in Tunisia or in a foreign country during the two years preceding the business relationship, high public functions or representative or political missions, and in particular:
- Head of State, Head of Government or member of a government,
- governors,
- member of a parliament, national and regional elected officials,
- member of a constitutional court or a high judiciary,
- member of a constitutional instance,
- military superior officers,
- Ambassador, chargé d'affaires or consul,
- members of administrative boards or councils of regulatory and control authorities and their first responsible,
- member of an administration, direction or control body of a public enterprise,
- members of the direction of an international institution created by treaty or the first responsible for its representation,
- high responsible of a political party,
- members of the organs of direction of a non-profit organization. Intermediary bank: any bank that receives and transmits an electronic funds transfer in a payment coverage series or chain, on behalf of the order giver's institution and the beneficiary's institution or another intermediary bank.

Electronic funds transfer: any operation performed electronically, through a national or foreign financial institution, on behalf of an order giver, to make funds available to a beneficiary through another financial institution. The order giver and beneficiary may be the same person.

Batch transfer: a set of several individual electronic funds transfers grouped for transmission.

Unique operation reference number: a combination of letters, numbers, or symbols defined according to the payment and settlement or messaging systems used to execute the electronic funds transfer and ensuring traceability of the transaction to the order giver and beneficiary.

Order giver: any person authorizing a funds transfer from an account or, in the absence of an account, issuing a funds transfer order.

Beneficiary: the intended recipient of the funds transfer.

Qualified transfer: any cross-border transfer of funds exceeding the countervalue of 1000 dinars. Title I: Vigilance Measures and Client/Operation Diligences
Chapter I: General Vigilance Measures

Article 3:
Besides the diligences provided by the CTAF Decision No. 2017-02, the subject establishments shall perform the diligences and observe the vigilance measures set forth in this circular.

Article 4:
The subject establishments shall take appropriate measures to identify, assess, and understand the risks of money laundering and terrorist financing to which they are exposed, taking into account risk factors such as the client profile, countries or geographical areas, products, services, transactions, or distribution channels.

The subject establishments shall:
- document their risk assessments;
- consider all relevant risk factors before determining the overall risk level and the level and type of appropriate measures to apply to mitigate those risks.

"Operation or transaction unusual": any operation or transaction that is complex in nature or involves an unusually large amount.

"Suspicious operation": any operation:
- that appears unrelated to the client's business activity;
- for which the documents or information indicating its purpose have not been produced;
- that lacks any apparent economic or legitimate justification. Six main points, notably the calibration of alert levels in relation to risk profiles; and:
- keeping evaluations up to date.

The subject establishment may, for the purpose of identifying money laundering and terrorist financing risks, rely on precise data related to its activity as well as information from the national risk assessment and reports published by international organizations.

The results of the risk assessment must be documented in a report called the "Risk Evaluation Report for Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing of the Subject Establishment". This report must break down the risk matrix by country, geographical zone, client type, product type, and distribution channel.

Article 5:

Subject establishments must verify the identity and business activity, as well as their financial environment, of any new client and/or their representative upon initiation of business relations. They must conduct an interview during the initial contact, with a client identification form (KYC) filled out by an authorized person, allowing:
- legal identification of the person;
- clear understanding of their activities, revenues, and assets;
- obtaining, for a corporate client, any indication of their business operations, through the communication of relevant information. 7

The elements of identification mentioned above should also be collected from people who may operate a client's account under power of attorney. These details must be substantiated by official documents, copies of which should not be kept in the client's file.

Article 6:

Institutions subject to this provision must carry out due diligence regarding the client's identity and, if applicable, the beneficiary of the transaction or operation and the capacity of the person acting on their behalf, particularly when:
- the client wishes to open an account, regardless of its nature, or rent a safe deposit box;
- the client conducts occasional transactions in cash, with a value equal to or exceeding 10,000 dinars or the equivalent of 5,000 dinars in foreign banknotes, in accordance with Circular No. 2012-11;
- the client conducts transactions in the form of electronic fund transfers;
- there is suspicion of money laundering or terrorism financing; and
- there are doubts about the authenticity or relevance of the client's previously obtained identification data.

Article 7:

Institutions subject to this provision must ensure the identity of significant associates and shareholders of their corporate clients and the effective beneficiaries.

The due diligence procedures mentioned above are simplified when the client Article 8:

Organic law for verifying the effective beneficiary's identity, notably by consulting relevant information or data from reliable sources. In this regard, they must:
- Determine, for all clients, if the client acts on behalf of a third party and take, if so, reasonable measures to obtain sufficient identification data to verify the third party's identity;
- Take, when the client is a legal entity or a legal construction, all reasonable measures to (a) understand the client's ownership and control structure; (b) determine who the natural persons are that ultimately own or exercise effective control over the client; and
- Ensure that the client is not a straw man or a shell company.

Article 9:

When subject establishments engage third parties to fulfill their client knowledge obligations, they must:
- Obtain necessary information about the third party's vigilance measures regarding clients immediately;
- Take appropriate measures to ensure that the third party can provide, upon request and within the shortest possible deadlines, copies of identification data and other relevant documents related to client vigilance duties;
- Ensure that the third party is subject to regulation and supervision regarding money laundering repression and counter-terrorism financing. 9.
An establishment subject to these provisions satisfies the obligations indicated above when the following conditions are met:
(a) the group applies measures of vigilance regarding clients and obligations of document retention, and anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing programs;
(b) the implementation of these vigilance measures regarding clients, document retention obligations, and anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing programs is controlled at the group level by a competent authority;
(c) any higher risks presented by the country are mitigated in a satisfactory manner by the group's anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing policies.

Article 10:
Subject institutions with foreign subsidiaries or branches must ensure that these entities take appropriate measures to protect against the risk of being used for money laundering and terrorist financing and are equipped with a vigilance mechanism at least equivalent to that provided for in this circular.

These subsidiaries and branches must communicate to the parent company, as necessary, the local applicable measures in host countries that oppose the implementation of all or part of the requirements set out in this circular.

When the obligations set out in this circular are not fully or partially implemented by the subsidiary or branch, the parent company must take all necessary measures to ensure compliance with these obligations. Article 11:
Establishments subject to this consolidated financial group must implement programs to combat money laundering and terrorist financing adapted to all their branches and subsidiaries in which they hold a majority participation. These programs include:
(a) policies and procedures for sharing required information for vigilance regarding clientele and risk management of money laundering and terrorist financing;
(b) making available information from branches and subsidiaries regarding clients, accounts, and operations when necessary for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing efforts, to compliance and audit functions at group level; and
(c) satisfactory guarantees in terms of confidentiality and use of exchanged information.

Article 12:
Establishments subject to this provision must exercise continuous vigilance throughout the business relationship. They must ensure that operations and assets placed with persons with whom they have a relationship are consistent with their knowledge of the client, their commercial activities, their risk profile, and, where applicable, the origin of the funds. Establishments subject to this provision must, therefore, ensure, through regular control, the updating and relevance of the documents, data or information collected during the customer due diligence process. Request for additional information from the client to ensure they are not suspicious as per the present circular.

Chapter II: Reinforced Vigilance Measures

Article 14:
Establishments subject to this requirement must, when concluding contracts with foreign banking correspondents and similar relationships, particularly those established for conducting securities transactions or electronic fund transfers, whether for their own account abroad or for their client's account:
- ensure that the correspondent is duly authorized and subject to the supervision of the competent authorities of their country of origin or the country where they are established;
- obtain sufficient information from the counterparty establishment regarding the nature of its activities and, based on publicly available and exploitable information, its reputation and the quality of supervision it is subject to;
- evaluate the anti-money laundering and terrorist financing measures put in place by the establishment, using a questionnaire whose model is attached in Annex 3 to the present circular;
- ensure that the decision to establish a business relationship with the counterparty establishment is made by the board of directors or executive management or a duly authorized person;
- have assurance, with regard to "pass-through" accounts, that the correspondent applies vigilance measures to clients having direct access. Article 15:
Established entities must exercise enhanced vigilance for identifying clients not residing in Tunisia. They must require, for instance, a reference letter delivered by their bank in their country of residence.

Article 16:
In addition to the measures provided by Chapter I of Title I, established entities must exercise enhanced vigilance for their relations with politically exposed persons. To this end, they must:
a) carry out necessary due diligence to determine if their client is one of the persons referred to in the first paragraph of this article;
b) obtain approval to establish or continue business relations with such a person, from the board of directors or the management or any other authorized person;
c) take reasonable measures to understand the origin of the client's assets; and
d) ensure enhanced and continuous monitoring of this relationship.

The same provisions apply to the close associates of the persons referred to in the first paragraph of this article and to persons having close relationships with them.

Direct family members, including ascendants and descendants up to the first degree and their spouses, are considered close associates of the persons mentioned above.

Any natural person known to have close business relationships with the mentioned persons is considered a person having close relationships with them. Established entities shall apply in addition to the measures provided in Chapter I of Title I, for clients acting as principal or beneficiary of enhanced due diligence measures, when:
- the client is a resident of countries identified by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) communiqués as countries not applying or not adequately applying the international anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing norms; and
- the transaction is carried out using new technologies of information and communication.

Article 18:
Established entities are obliged, in their business dealings and transactions with natural and legal persons from countries identified by the FATF as countries not applying or not adequately applying the international anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing norms, to apply proportionate counter-measures, notably:
- to systematically declare suspicious transactions;
- to apply enhanced due diligence measures. Article 14:
Prohibition of using third parties established in the concerned country to perform certain elements of the vigilance process regarding the client.

Article 20:
Establishments subject to this Regulation shall implement a system enabling the identification and assessment of risks related to the use of new technologies for money laundering or terrorist financing purposes. To this end, they shall be equipped with risk management systems allowing for the identification and assessment of money laundering or terrorist financing risks arising:
- from the development of new products and services, including new distribution channels; and
- from the use of new or emerging technologies in connection with new or existing products.

The risk assessment referred to in the first subparagraph of this Article shall be carried out before the launch of new products or services or before the use of new or emerging technologies. Establishments subject to this Regulation shall take appropriate measures to manage and mitigate these risks as well as those specific risks linked to business relationships and transactions not involving the physical presence of the parties.

Article 21:
Establishments subject to this Regulation shall apply enhanced due diligence to any transaction or operation:
- which appears to have no relation to the client’s business;
- for which the documents or information indicating its purpose have not been provided; or
- which involves high-risk countries or high-risk sectors. 15

Establishments subject to examination shall review the framework in which operations or transactions requiring enhanced vigilance are carried out and shall record the results of this examination in writing and make them available to the Central Bank of Tunisia and the auditors.

Chapter III : Specific Vigilance Measures Regarding Electronic Funds Transfer Operations

Article 22 :
The vigilance measures provided for in this chapter apply to all electronic funds transfer operations, regardless of currency, that are initiated or received by a bank or financial institution. They do not apply, however, to the following transfers:
a) made using credit or debit cards for the purchase of goods or services, provided that the card number accompanies all transfers resulting from the operation;
b) made on behalf of a public administration for the payment of taxes, fines, or other deductions; and
c) for which the issuer and beneficiary are both banks or financial institutions acting on their own behalf.

Section I : Diligences to be Observed by the Ordering Establishment
Article 23:
The establishment subject to the orderer shall ensure that international transfers contain the following exact and complete information about the orderer:
a) the name and first name of the orderer. a) the name and surname of the beneficiary; and
b) the beneficiary's bank or postal account number or, in the absence of an account, a unique operation reference number enabling traceability of the transaction.

International transfers not qualifying as funds transfers must contain the name and surname of the order giver and the beneficiary, as well as each party's account number or unique operation reference number. The order giver's establishment may not verify the accuracy of these details, except in cases of suspected money laundering or terrorism financing.

Article 24:

The order giver's establishment verifies the accuracy of the information specified in Article 23 of this circular before issuing a qualified international transfer, based on documents, data, or reliable information from a source.

The verification referred to in the first paragraph of this article is considered to have been completed. Article 25:
The issuer of the order must refuse to execute any international fund transfers if the required information is incomplete or missing.

Article 26:
When multiple cross-border electronic transfers originating from the same orderer are transmitted in batches to beneficiaries, they may be exempted from the obligations regarding orderer information under article 23 of this circular, provided they contain the orderer's account number or unique operation reference number and the batch includes complete and accurate information on the orderer, as well as complete information on the beneficiaries. The entire trail of these information must be reconstructable in the receiving country.

Article 27:
Domestic fund transfers must include the information specified in article 23 of this circular, except when this information can be made available:
a) by the beneficiary's institution or the Central Bank of Tunisia through any other means within 3 business days following receipt by the orderer's institution, or
b) by judicial authorities upon request.

In such cases, the orderer's institution only includes the account number or a unique operation reference number enabling the reconstruction of the transfer trail. Section II: Obligations for Intermediary Banks

Article 28:
An intermediary bank must ensure that all information about the order giver and beneficiary accompanying an electronic transfer remain attached. When technical ordering constraints prevent the required information about the order giver or beneficiary from being transmitted with the corresponding electronic transfer, the intermediary bank is required to keep the received information from the order giver's bank or another intermediary bank for at least ten years.

Article 29:
An intermediary bank must implement appropriate procedures to detect if, in the messaging or payment and settlement system used to execute the funds transfer, the fields intended to contain the order giver and beneficiary information have been filled in using unauthorized characters or elements, according to the system's conventions.

Article 30:
An intermediary bank must have policies and procedures based on risk assessment to decide whether to execute, suspend, request additional information, or reject funds transfers where required information about the order giver and beneficiary is missing or incomplete, or the fields concerning these informations have not been filled in using authorized characters or elements. Article 19:

The intermediary bank must report this omission and the measures taken to the Central Bank of Tunisia.

Article 32:
The intermediary bank assesses, based on incomplete or missing information about the order giver or beneficiary, whether the funds transfer, or any related transaction, has a suspicious character and must be reported to the CTAF.

Section III: Duties of the Beneficiary Establishment

Article 33:
The beneficiary establishment must apply appropriate procedures to detect if, in the Swift messaging system or the payment and settlement system used to process the funds transfer, the fields intended to contain information about the order giver and beneficiary have been completed using acceptable characters or elements according to the system's conventions.

Article 34:
For qualified fund transfers in currencies, the beneficiary establishment must, for single transaction or multiple transactions that appear related, verify the accuracy of the beneficiary information before crediting their account or making the funds available to them, and when this has not been done previously. Article 35:
The beneficiary establishment is not required to verify the accuracy of the beneficiary information for non-qualified fund transfers in currencies that do not appear related to other fund transfers and whose total amount, combined with that of the transfer in question, exceeds the counter-value of 1000 dinars, unless:
a) the funds are paid in cash
b) it has reasonable grounds to suspect money laundering or terrorist financing activities.

Article 36:
The beneficiary establishment must have policies and procedures based on risk to decide on the appropriateness of executing, suspending, or requesting additional information or rejecting fund transfers whose required information on the order giver and beneficiary is missing or incomplete or whose relevant fields have not been filled in with the required characters or admissible elements according to the messaging or payment system conventions.

Article 37:
The beneficiary establishment takes reasonable measures to detect cross-border electronic transfers for which required information on the order giver or beneficiary is missing, notably through post-transaction control or, when possible, real-time control.

When an establishment repeatedly fails to provide the required information on the order giver or beneficiary, the beneficiary establishment shall take appropriate measures. Article 38:
The beneficiary establishment should decide, based on missing or incomplete information, whether to report to the CTAF, in accordance with article 58 of this circular, the transfer or transaction related to it.

Chapter IV: Prohibitions
Article 39:

When subjected establishments cannot verify the identification data of their clients or the information collected is insufficient or manifestly fictitious, they must refrain from opening accounts, establishing or continuing business relationships, or performing the operation or transaction and consider filing a suspicion report.

Article 40:
Subjected establishments must refuse to establish or continue a correspondent banking relationship with a fictitious bank.

Article 41:
Subjected establishments must refuse to establish relationships with foreign financial institutions that allow fictitious banks to use accounts opened on their ledgers.

Article 42:
Subjected establishments are prohibited, in accordance with article 98 of the Organic Law, from providing any form of support and financing, directly or indirectly, through physical or legal persons, to persons, organizations, or activities related to terrorist offenses and other illicit activities. Article 43:
Subjected establishments shall not maintain anonymous or fictitious accounts.

Title II: Internal Control System
Chapter I: Rules for Internal Control in Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing Management

Article 44:
Subjected establishments shall have an organization, human and logistical resources, and clear and precise internal procedures to ensure proper application and respect of legal and regulatory provisions in the fight against money laundering and terrorism financing. The procedures mentioned above are an integral part of the internal control system as defined by article 3 of circular no. 2006-19 and must describe the required diligences and rules, particularly in matters of:
- client identification and knowledge;
- establishment and updating of client files;
- determination of verification identity of clients and updating related information; these deadlines must be more frequent for clients subject to enhanced vigilance;
- execution of electronic funds transfer operations;
- establishment of relationships with foreign correspondent banks;
- surveillance and examination of unusual operations and transactions; the results must be documented in writing and made available to the Central Bank of Tunisia. 23.
- analysis of operations or transactions subject to a declaration of suspicion pursuant to Article 125 of the Organic Law;
- document retention; and
- database constitution and conservation.
Internal procedures must be examined and approved by the audit committee and approved by the administrative council or supervisory board of the subject establishment.

Article 45:
The risk of money laundering and terrorism financing must be included in the risk mapping at the level at which the risk committee assists the administrative council or supervisory board in the design and updating of an appropriate management strategy and the setting of management and control rules.

Article 46:
Subject establishments are required to put in place formalized, clear, and quick procedures for:
- subordinating the payment of funds, to any moral person subject to a restriction on receiving foreign wires, with prior authorization from the Minister in charge of Finances pursuant to Article 102 of the Organic Law; and
- executing decisions taken in the context of Article 103 of the Organic Law regarding the freezing of assets of persons or organizations whose link with terrorist crimes is established by competent international institutions.

Article 47:
Subject establishments must be equipped with an information system allowing:
- profiling. 24
- to identify transactions with suspicious or unusual characteristics.

Establishments subject to this must take into account any element likely to change the client's profile.

Article 48:
Establishments must establish, for each category of clients, detection rules for money laundering operations, including thresholds beyond which operations could be considered unusual or suspicious. These thresholds must also take into account the risk of transaction fragmentation.

Article 49:
The information system provided for in Article 47 of the present circular must be periodically examined for its effectiveness in adapting it to the nature and evolution of the establishment's activity and the legal and regulatory environment.

Article 50:
Establishments subject to this must ensure permanent and periodic rigorous control, as per Article 7 of Circular No. 2006-19 on the proper application of internal procedures referred to in Article 44 of the present circular. The internal control system for managing the money laundering risk must be audited according to a frequency that takes into account the nature, volume, and complexity of the establishment's operations and, in any case, at least once every two years. The terms of reference for the audit missions of the internal control system for managing the money laundering risk must be revalidated by the audit committee. The audit conclusions must be [validated]. 25

Article 51:
Subject institutions must keep the files of their permanent or occasional clients and the related identity documents for a period of at least ten years starting from the end of the relationship.

They must also keep the documents and information relating to the operations and transactions carried out on their behalf electronically and/or on paper for a minimum period of 10 years starting from the date of their execution, considering the possibility of their consultation by competent authorities.

Article 52:
The organization of document retention must enable the reconstruction of all transactions and the provision of required information to authorized entities in a timely manner.

Article 53:
Subject institutions must define the rules of ethics and professional conduct regarding the declaration of suspicion, including those related to the confidentiality obligation.

These rules are an integral part of the Code of Ethics provided by Article 6 of Circular No. 2011-06 on strengthening good governance in credit establishments.

Article 54:
The statutory auditors of institutions are required to evaluate the internal control system for managing the money laundering risk as prescribed by law and regulation.

Their conclusions must be recorded in their reports addressed to the Central Bank of Tunisia and must include, among other things: with the degree of exposure of the establishment to this risk in relation to its nature, volume and complexity of its activity.

Article 55:

Internal procedures for fighting money laundering and terrorism financing, as provided for in article 44 of the present circular, must be made known to staff in contact with clients and all concerned staff.

Article 56:

Establishments subject to these provisions must set up a continuous training program for employees, including information on techniques, methods and trends in fighting money laundering and terrorism financing. This training must cover all aspects of the regulation and in particular the obligations regarding vigilance towards clients and transactions, and the declaration of suspicious transactions and operations.

Chapter II: On the declaration of suspicion
Article 57:

The person designated as the CTAF representative in accordance with the provisions of article 13 of the CTAF decision No. 2017-2 and their substitute must be part of the permanent control body.

Agents in charge of examining unusual or suspicious operations or transactions subject to control must have appropriate professional qualifications. At least one of these agents must have obtained a professional diploma in anti-money laundering. Article 58:
Subject institutions must declare suspicious operations and transactions in accordance with the model set out in the CTAF Decision No. 2017-01 of March 2, 2017.
They are also required to declare any attempt to carry out such operations or transactions.
The declaration obligation applies, equally, even after the operation or transaction has been completed, when new information becomes available that can directly or indirectly link the said operation or transaction to funds derived from criminal or illicit activities as defined by law, or to the financing of persons, organizations or activities related to terrorist offenses.

Chapter III: Central Bank of Tunisia Information

Article 59:
Subject institutions must submit to the Central Bank of Tunisia (Banking Supervision General Directorate) no later than one month after the end of each exercise, a document conforming to the annex 5 of the present circular, which indicates:
- the total number of declarations made to the CTAF during the closed exercise; and
- the total amount of declared operations during the closed exercise, broken down by type of operation and category of clientele (physical persons and legal entities).

Article 60:
Subject institutions shall include in their internal control report, which they are required to submit to the Central Bank of Tunisia in accordance with article 50 of circular No. 28
 The evaluation report on money laundering and terrorist financing risks, as required by article 4 of the present circular, must be communicated to the Central Bank of Tunisia by the end of September 2018. Any update to this report must also be communicated to the Central Bank of Tunisia.

Article 61:
Any failure to comply with the obligations set out in this circular exposes the concerned establishment to the disciplinary sanctions provided by law No. 2016-48 on banks and financial institutions.

Article 62:
Establishments subject to these provisions have a six-month period to comply with the provisions of Chapter III of Title I of the present circular.

Article 63:
